    18. Convolution#

    In the notes 14. Dense subclasses of , we met the convolution of and . There, Hölder’s inequality made the integral converge for every , and approximation by continuous functions with compact support showed that is continuous. The value is an average of the values of near , weighted by : for , it is the mean value of on the ball , because exactly when . Averages of this kind are defined in many situations in which Hölder’s inequality does not apply, for example for two functions in , and the question is then in what sense the integral exists and how large the result is.

    For each fixed , the convolution is an integral in whose integrand depends on the parameter . Regarded as a function of both variables, the integrand lives on the product , and Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems (Theorem 16.1, Theorem 17.1) give its integrals in both orders. In these notes, we use them to show that the convolution of two integrable functions is defined almost everywhere and integrable, and that convolution with an integrable function maps into itself for every .

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Define the convolution of two measurable functions, and prove with Tonelli’s theorem that the set where it is defined and the resulting function are measurable.

    • Compute the convolution of two indicator functions and interpret it as an average of translates.

    • Prove that the convolution of two functions in is defined almost everywhere and satisfies , and give an example where it is not defined everywhere.

    • Prove that convolution is commutative by a change of variables.

    • Prove Young’s inequality for from Minkowski’s integral inequality, and interpret it as Minkowski’s inequality for an -weighted integral of translates.

    • Express the measure of the overlap as a convolution, and use its continuity to prove that contains a ball around when (Steinhaus’s theorem); explain why need not be open, and why contains a ball around some point.

    Throughout these notes, carries Lebesgue measure on the Borel -algebra , integrals are taken with respect to , and . Functions on are Borel measurable with values in . Every Lebesgue measurable function agrees almost everywhere with a Borel measurable function (we use this fact without proof), so this convention does not change the spaces ; it ensures that compositions such as are measurable on . By Corollary 15.11, and is Lebesgue measure on , so Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems apply on .

    18.1 Definition of the convolution#

    18.1.1 Translations, reflections, and the change of variables#

By the translation and reflection invariance of Lebesgue measure (14.5), for every Borel function and every , Indeed, the function is the reflection of the translate , and both operations preserve the integral. Applying (18.1) to and extends it to every integrable . With , it shows that is a null set whenever is a Borel null set.

    18.2 Convolution of integrable functions#

    For , Hölder’s inequality gives no information about at a fixed , since a product of two integrable functions need not be integrable. Instead, we integrate the convolution integrand over both variables. Tonelli’s theorem computes this double integral, and its finiteness implies, through Fubini’s theorem, that almost every section is integrable.

    Warning (A convolution of integrable functions that is not defined everywhere)#

    Let for and , so that , and on let . As in the computation of the tent, Tonelli’s theorem integrates a non-negative product one coordinate at a time, so and . At , the integrand is again a product, , and so . The two factors of the integrand blow up on the same coordinate hyperplanes , and their product is not integrable. By Proposition 18.3, such points form a null set. In contrast, for and with conjugate exponents, Hölder’s inequality shows that the convolution is defined at every point (Theorem 14.10).

    18.4 Young’s inequality for convolutions#

    18.4.1 An explanation by Minkowski’s inequality#

    Let us first replace the integral in (18.8) by a finite sum. For finitely many translations and weights , Minkowski’s inequality (Theorem 11.13) and the translation invariance give A finite combination of translates of is therefore no larger in than , multiplied by the total weight . The convolution is a continuous analogue of such a combination: if we cut into small cubes with centers , the integral (18.8) resembles the sum , whose total weight resembles . The estimate (18.9) then suggests . Minkowski’s integral inequality (Theorem 16.8), which is Minkowski’s inequality with the sum replaced by an integral, turns this heuristic into a proof, without any approximation by sums.

    Remark 18.7 (Convolution as an -weighted integral of translates)#

    Young’s inequality is Minkowski’s inequality for the integral (18.8), read as an integral whose values are functions. For each , the translate is an element of the normed space , so is a function on with values in ; for , the translates depend continuously on (Theorem 14.8). In this reading, is an integral of a vector-valued function, a “sum” of the vectors with the weights , and Young’s inequality is the triangle inequality for this integral, “the norm of the integral is at most the integral of the norm”: For a finite sum, this is (18.9).

    Integrals of functions with values in a normed space can be defined directly, by approximation with vector-valued simple functions, for which the triangle inequality is Minkowski’s inequality; we do not develop this theory in the course. The product-space theory provides it in the case at hand. An -valued function of is described by the function of two variables, its vector-valued integral is evaluated one point at a time by integrating in , and Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems guarantee that the result is a measurable function of whose integrals can be computed in either order. In this sense, Fubini’s theorem is a concrete form of vector-valued integration, and Minkowski’s integral inequality (Theorem 16.8) is the corresponding triangle inequality. The same reading gives the estimate for in the notes 19. Approximate identities and mollification: there, is the vector-valued integral of the differences .

    For with , the formula (18.8) expresses as a weighted average of the translates of , and Young’s inequality states that this average is no larger than in the norm. This is the situation studied in the notes 19. Approximate identities and mollification.

    Remark 18.8 (Two kinds of information about a convolution)#

    Young’s inequality and the results on in the notes 14. Dense subclasses of give different information about a convolution.

    • For and , Theorem 18.6 gives : the convolution is as integrable as . The proof integrates in both variables and uses Tonelli’s theorem, through Minkowski’s integral inequality.

    • For and with , Theorem 14.10 gives : the convolution is defined everywhere, bounded, and continuous. The proof applies Hölder’s inequality at each point , and approximation by functions in . For and , the convolution is bounded and uniformly continuous (Remark 14.11).

    For and , both apply, and Theorem 18.6 for recovers the bound of Remark 14.11.

    18.5 Sums and differences of sets#

    Convolutions of indicator functions measure how much a set overlaps with its translates. In this section, we use this to show that a set of positive measure has many differences: for with , every point near is a difference of two points of . For , a set of positive measure need not contain any interval: if is open in , contains every rational number of , and has measure , such as the fat rationals of Definition 1.21 with , then has positive measure and contains no interval, because every interval contains a rational number. The set of differences of a set of positive measure, however, always contains an interval.
